textRuns.value: 1 MUSIC: Popular songs are mid-tempo (median ~121 BPM), danceable (~69%) and energetic (~66%). Danceability and valence correlate (+0.40 Spearman). Audio features barely differ between bigger and smaller hits (|rho| <= 0.11 with streams).

2 CROSS-PLATFORM: Apple Music has the widest chart reach (90% of songs), then Shazam (59%), Spotify (58%), Deezer (42%). 271 songs (29%) chart on all four platforms; median streams stop rising after ~3 platforms.

3 PLAYLISTS: Playlist exposure is the strongest correlate of streams (Spearman 0.83; log-log R2 0.62). Top-quartile songs have ~9x the median streams of the bottom quartile. Association, not proof of causation - popular songs also attract playlists.
4 CHARTS: Chart presence is moderately related to streams (rho 0.12-0.34). Apple Music is most informative; Shazam behaves like a discovery signal (High tier median below Mid tier).

5 OUTLIERS: 26 over-performers (older, more acoustic, low playlists) and 40 under-performers (mostly 2022-23 releases with many playlists but low streams). Explanations such as catalogue/sync effects and new-release lag are interpretations, not proven by the data.
6 ARTISTS: 213 of 698 artists (30.5%) generate 80% of streams; top 10% of artists hold 52%, top 20% hold 69%. Concentrated but not a strict 80/20 because the data contains only hit songs.

Chart columns are treated as a presence score (0 = not charted; higher = stronger). Collaborations are credited in full to each artist, so artist totals overlap. Missing Shazam values set to 0. One corrupted streams row removed; 4 duplicate songs de-duplicated (kept higher streams). Correlations here use Pearson on log scale; the report quotes Spearman.
Single snapshot (no time series), only successful songs, Spotify streams only, no forecasting. Measure/column definitions are in the semantic model (Songs and ArtistSongs tables).
